nameStory: The 'agilis' in this spider's scientific name comes from Latin meaning 'quick' or 'agile,' hinting at this little hunter's speedy movements. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, it belongs to the comb-tailed spider family, named for the row of curved bristles (called a calamistrum) on their hind legs that looks like a tiny comb.
description: This is a very small, inconspicuous spider that most people walk right past without noticing. Comb-tailed spiders are typically less than 3mm long - about the size of a peppercorn - with brownish coloration that helps them blend into leaf litter and soil. They're part of a family known for building distinctive woolly webs close to the ground, though individual species can be quite challenging to identify without magnification.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny - usually under 3mm long, smaller than your pinky nail and easily overlooked among fallen leaves

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small, woolly-textured sheet webs close to the ground that feel slightly fuzzy or cotton-like when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with relatively long legs for its tiny body size, giving it a delicate appearance

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brownish or grayish coloration that blends with soil and dead leaves - specific patterns require magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves quickly when disturbed, darting away with surprising speed for such a small spider

habitat: Look for this tiny spider in leaf litter, under logs, and in the upper layers of forest soil where organic matter accumulates. They prefer moist, shaded areas in deciduous and mixed forests where their small webs can be built among decomposing leaves and small twigs.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, with peak activity often in late spring when they're searching for mates and building webs.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for hunting and web-building, though their tiny size makes them difficult to spot even when abundant.
seasonality.fall: May still be active in early fall, but begin preparing for winter by seeking shelter in deeper leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters in protected locations under bark, logs, or deep in leaf litter where they remain dormant until spring.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most people's fingernail, comb-tailed spiders produce some of the most complex silk in the spider world - they use their specialized 'comb' to card their silk into a woolly texture that's incredibly effective at trapping tiny prey like springtails and mites.
confusionNotes: Due to their tiny size and brownish coloration, these spiders are easily confused with juvenile spiders of many other families. The key difference is their distinctive woolly, sheet-like webs - most other small spiders either don't build webs or build different web types like orb webs or simple tangles.
contextualKnowledge: This species is so rarely reported that it may be more common than records suggest - their tiny size means they're likely overlooked by most casual observers and even many researchers. The single observation count in New England probably reflects detection difficulty rather than true rarity.
compareHints: Distinguishing Neoantistea agilis from its relative the Thick-hooked Comb-tailed Spider (N. magna) requires expert examination, as both are extremely small and similar-looking. The main differences involve microscopic features of their reproductive structures and subtle variations in their web-spinning apparatus that aren't visible to casual observers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Distinguishing this species from its relative Neoantistea agilis requires expert examination of microscopic features, particularly the male's reproductive structures that give this species its 'thick-hooked' name.
